verses.note: Homage to the son is homage to God, since rebellion against one was rebellion against both (verse 2). The New Testament presents every knee bowing to the exalted Christ to the glory of God the Father (Philippians 2:9-11).

Peter moves from this verse to Christ exalted to the right hand of God (Acts 2:33-34), connecting the psalm's ‘right hand’ with Psalm 110:1. The one not abandoned to Sheol now sits in the place of pleasures forever.

Because the figure travels to the Ancient of Days, some interpreters, including N. T. Wright (Jesus and the Victory of God, 1996), argue that Jesus' use of the verse speaks first of his vindication and enthronement, fulfilled in his resurrection and ascension, rather than only of a descent to earth.

The universal service given to this figure is the Old Testament background for Philippians 2:9-11, where every knee bows and every tongue confesses Jesus as Lord. The early church's worship of Christ drew on texts like this one in which God shares his kingdom and honor with a human figure at his side.
